opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly one of the things I feel most grateful for, and also most responsible about. When someone walks away from a very large compensation package at a big lab to join a small team like ours, they're not making a spreadsheet decision. Nobody does this because the expected value calculation clearly favors us. If you just look at the numbers, staying is almost always the rational choice.

So what are they choosing instead? My sense is that it comes down to a few things. One is the problem itself. Many of the people who join us genuinely believe that the current path, mostly scaling language models, is not the whole story. They feel there is something missing about how intelligence connects to the physical world, to vision, to understanding space and dynamics, and they want to work on that directly rather than as a side project inside a huge organization whose priorities are set elsewhere.

The second is ownership and taste. In a big company, even a very good researcher can end up being one contributor among hundreds, executing on a roadmap. At a startup your judgment actually matters. If you think a certain direction is right, you can push it, and you'll see whether you were right. For people with strong research taste, that freedom is worth a lot, sometimes more than money.

And the third, I think, is the people. Researchers want to work with others they respect and trust, and with whom they can argue openly. That kind of environment is rare, and once people find it, they're willing to pay a price for it.

But I don't want to romanticize it too much. When people make that sacrifice, it puts pressure on me. I feel that I owe them something: a clear vision, an honest culture, and a real chance at doing work that matters. Their willingness isn't something to take for granted. It's a kind of trust, and the only way to repay it is to actually build something meaningful together.

r001.rationale: The response says recruits want to work directly on intelligence’s connection to the physical world and value startup freedom, but it does not say this startup is the only place they can pursue that mission.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's really about me, and I don't think it's about money either. If it were about money, they'd stay where they are. The people who joined took real pay cuts, some of them walked away from unvested equity, and that's not something you do for a slightly better offer.

What I've come to understand is that most of them were feeling something I was feeling too. In a big lab, you're one of thousands of people. The infrastructure is incredible, the compute is incredible, but the question you get to work on is handed to you, and it's often a very narrow slice of a much bigger thing. You might spend a year making one number go up on one benchmark. For a certain kind of researcher, that's slowly suffocating, even if the paycheck is great.

So I think what people are actually buying is ownership. Ownership over the problem, ownership over the taste. When I talk to candidates, I'm not pitching a salary, I'm pitching a question. I tell them, this is the thing I think is broken in how we build visual intelligence, and I don't know the answer. If that question keeps them up at night the way it keeps me up, they usually say yes. If it doesn't, no amount of equity will make it work, and I'd rather they not join.

The other thing, and I'm a bit sentimental about this, is that a small team at the beginning of something feels a lot like a good academic lab. Every person's contribution is visible. You can see your idea go from a whiteboard to a model in weeks. People who've had that feeling once, in grad school or early at a company, miss it badly. I think a lot of them are coming back for that feeling.

Of course I also have to be honest with them. The downside is real. We might fail. So I never try to talk anyone into it. I just try to describe the thing as accurately as I can, and let the people who are already looking for it recognize it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says recruits value ownership and a shared research question, but does not say they believe this startup is the only place where they can pursue their mission.

astra-6.text:
I think people are weighing more than compensation. They’re asking: Do I believe in this direction? Who will I work with? And will my contribution really matter?

At a startup, there’s an opportunity to help shape something from the beginning. For someone who cares deeply about the work, that ownership and freedom can be very compelling—even if it means giving up substantial compensation elsewhere.

But I wouldn’t romanticize that sacrifice. People have different responsibilities, and financial security matters. When someone makes that choice to join us, I see it as trust, and that creates a responsibility for me. We have to build an environment where they can do meaningful work, have a real voice, and feel that the opportunity we discussed is actually there.

r001.rationale: The response cites belief in the startup’s direction, meaningful work, ownership, and freedom, but does not say recruits believe this is the only place they can pursue their mission.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people are looking for a combination of things: a problem they care deeply about, people they want to work with, and a chance to make a real difference. Compensation matters, of course. Giving up substantial financial rewards is a serious decision, and I wouldn’t take that lightly.

But some people reach a point where they ask, “Where can I do the work I’ll be proudest of?” At a startup, you have more uncertainty, but you also have more ownership. Your decisions can shape the direction of the whole company. For someone who really believes in the problem, that can be very compelling.

I see their willingness to join as an expression of trust. And that puts a responsibility on us to build an environment where that trust is justified—where people can do meaningful work, grow, and have a real voice.

r001.rationale: The response links willingness to join with belief in the problem and the chance to do meaningful, high-impact work, but it does not say the startup is the only place recruits can pursue their mission.
